profile.summary: MF-PCBA is a set of 60 drug screening data sets assembled from PubChem BioAssay, each pairing two measurement qualities for the same project: a large, noisy primary screen at a single concentration, and the much smaller dose-response confirmation of the compounds that came through it. The prediction task is regression on the dose-response values, and the point of the benchmark is whether a model can use the hundreds of thousands of primary measurements to predict the few thousand confirmatory ones better than it could from the confirmatory data alone. The collection holds over 16.6 million unique compound and target interactions and over 1.1 million unique compounds, with five fixed random splits per data set. It is for people building molecular property prediction methods, particularly transfer learning between cheap and expensive measurements.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether low-quality data helps. In a real screening campaign a library is tested once at a single dose, then the hits are retested over a dose range to get a reliable potency. Machine learning work usually models only the second, small set and throws the first away. MF-PCBA keeps both and asks for predictions of the dose-response values, so a method is judged on whether it can turn hundreds of thousands of noisy single-dose measurements into better predictions of a few thousand reliable ones. The authors describe the training sets for the confirmatory-only task as typically fewer than 2000 instances, against primary screens orders of magnitude larger. They also point out that the relationship between the two is not simply strong: the per-data-set correlation between paired single-dose and dose-response values is printed for every one of the 60 sets, and it includes weak and negative values.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The 60 projects were found by hand, searching PubChem BioAssay for primary and confirmatory screening terms, because the two halves of a campaign may sit in one assay or in two and the formats differ. The assays date from 2008 to 2018. Everything after the selection is automated through PubChem's REST interface: the assay rows are downloaded by identifier, SMILES strings are fetched per compound, replicate primary measurements are averaged by mean, with a median option in the code, and dose-response values reported as half maximal concentrations or their logarithms are converted to pXC50. Four RDKit filtering steps follow: sanitisation, keeping the largest fragment to drop counterions, removing stereochemistry and then deduplicating on SMILES, which makes the task modelling racemic mixtures, and neutralising charges. The paper reports how many compounds each step removed on average. Each finished data set holds the compound identifier, the SMILES string and the single-dose and dose-response activity values, with PubChem's binary activity labels included, and five random 80, 10, 10 splits of the dose-response data are provided with their seeds published.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: One model per data set: the authors say they consider only single-task learning, so a separate model is trained for each of the 60 sets. The recommended comparison is between a dose-response-only model, trained on confirmatory data alone, and a model that also uses the primary data, so that any gain can be attributed to the extra modality. The paper's own evaluation uses two ways of adding the primary information: appending the measured single-dose value to the compound's feature vector, and training a graph neural network on all the primary data and appending the embedding it produces, which also works for molecules it never saw. For the dose-response regression the authors recommend the coefficient of determination together with an error metric, mean absolute error or root mean square error; for the classification form of the task, the Matthews correlation coefficient together with the area under the ROC curve. Their reported numbers come from random forests, support vector machines and graph neural networks for the confirmatory step, with graph networks for the primary step, over the five provided splits.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The data are not distributed as a file: the repository downloads and rebuilds them from PubChem. Install Python 3.9 or later with pandas, numpy, rdkit, tqdm and scipy, then call the retrieval script with the primary assay identifier, the names of the columns holding the single-dose and dose-response values, the transformation to apply to the dose-response values, the confirmatory assay identifier when it is a separate assay, and an output directory. Ready-made scripts for all 60 data sets are in the retrieve-scripts directory, and the authors note they can be run in parallel. A notebook then splits the dose-response data into train, validation and test sets five times using the published seeds, writing one numbered directory per split. The paper reports that rebuilding one data set of 335,445 primary molecules took 554.52 seconds on the machine described.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 60 multifidelity data sets, each a primary single-dose screen paired with its dose-response confirmation, drawn from PubChem BioAssay with assay dates from 2008 to 2018. In total over 16.6 million unique compound and target interactions and over 1.1 million unique compounds. Table 1 of the paper lists every data set with its assay identifiers, assay type, measurement types, unfiltered sizes and the correlation between the paired measurements; primary screen sizes there run to the hundreds of thousands and confirmatory sets to the hundreds or low thousands. The collection is also split into MF-PCBA-23, the previously analysed subset, and the disjoint MF-PCBA-37.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Deduplication and an overlap check, but no structural split. Stereochemistry is removed and molecules are deduplicated on SMILES within a data set, so the same structure cannot appear twice. The splits are random over compounds, not by scaffold or by cluster, so analogues can fall on both sides. The authors do check overlap with other collections: no assay in common with the 128 assays of PCBA, 27 confirmatory assays in common with the 1310 assays of an earlier ChEMBL-derived set, and no overlap in primary assays. Overlap between the 60 data sets themselves is limited, with over 75.6 per cent of values missing if all compounds are matched against all primary screens.

facts.value: A molecule in one screening project. facts.value: Mostly inapplicable: the examples are small molecules and the labels are activity against a target or in a cell or organism assay, not sequences from a species. facts.label: Assays
facts.value: High-throughput screening data from PubChem of two kinds. Primary screens are single-concentration measurements, reported as percent inhibition, percent activity or a B-score at a stated concentration, sometimes with replicates, which are averaged. Confirmatory screens are dose-response measurements reported as half maximal inhibitory, activity or effective concentrations, or their logarithms, all converted to pXC50. Assay types in Table 1 include biochemical, cell-based and whole-organism readouts.

structured.split: five random 80, 10, 10 splits of the dose-response data, seeds published
structured.primary_metric: Matthews correlation coefficient, with the area under the ROC curve

quotes.text: the prediction problem can be naturally formulated as a supervised regression task. At the same time, the binary activity labels from PubChem are included for each dataset.

coupled with an error metric such as the mean absolute error (MAE) or root-mean-square error (RMSE) for regression tasks and the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) coupled with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for classification.
Furthermore, we provide five random splits per dataset (80%/10%/10% split ratios for the train/validation/test sets) for the DR data.

notes: The 16.6 million figure is the whole collection's count of unique compound and target interactions, not a test set: the test set is 10 per cent of each data set's dose-response rows, and no saved file prints those counts, which sit in Table 1 of the paper. 1.1 million is the number of unique compounds in the collection. The 60 data sets split into MF-PCBA-23, analysed in earlier work, and the disjoint MF-PCBA-37 that this paper added, and the paper's results focus on the 37. The data are not distributed: the MIT licensed repository rebuilds them from PubChem, so a rebuilt copy depends on PubChem at the time of running, and no licence is stated for the assembled data. The paper is CC BY 4.0. The repository's README points to a separate repository for the multifidelity modelling code, which was not fetched.
